# Hash-pinned install set for windows-enterprise-tls.yml / e2e.
#
# Direct requirements: pytest mitmproxy requests
#
# mitmproxy is the reason this file exists. The job stands it up as a real
# TLS-interception proxy and puts its generated root CA into the actual
# Windows certificate store, so for the length of the run mitmproxy is a
# TRUSTED ISSUER for every HTTPS call the runner makes. That is the whole
# point of the scenario, and it is also why an unpinned resolve here is worse
# than an unpinned resolve almost anywhere else in this repo: the package
# being installed from whatever the index served that minute is the package
# handed the authority to sign for any host. pytest and requests ride along
# in the same install -- requests is not a package dependency,
# tests/conftest.py imports it.
#
# Installed with `pip install --require-hashes`, which refuses to install
# anything not listed here with a matching hash -- so the job gets the exact
# artifacts this file names, or it fails. Every transitive dependency is
# present because --require-hashes demands the whole closure; that is the
# point, not padding.
#
# Each version lists the sha256 of EVERY distribution PyPI publishes for it
# (wheels for each platform, plus the sdist). pip accepts a download that
# matches any one of them, so the pin does not quietly depend on the runner
# resolving to the same wheel this file was generated against.
#
# Updating: Dependabot owns the routine bumps (see the /.github/requirements
# pip entry in .github/dependabot.yml) and rewrites the hashes with them. A
# pin with no updater is the frozen end of the same problem an unpinned
# install is at the other end of.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# RESOLVED FOR WINDOWS / CPython 3.13, unlike the rest of this directory.
#
# This job runs on windows-latest at Python 3.13 (the customer environment it
# reproduces), and this closure CANNOT be produced by pointing pip at a
# Windows platform tag from a Linux box. `pip --platform win_amd64` still
# evaluates environment markers against the interpreter doing the resolving,
# so on Linux it is wrong in both directions at once:
#
#   * it DROPS `pydivert; sys_platform == "win32"` -- a real Windows
#     dependency of mitmproxy -- because that marker reads False; and
#   * it DEMANDS `mitmproxy-linux; sys_platform == "linux"` (a dependency of
#     mitmproxy-rs) because that marker reads True. mitmproxy-linux publishes
#     no Windows distribution, so every mitmproxy 12.x is rejected and the
#     resolve lands silently on 11.0.2 with cryptography 44.
#
# Both failures are silent and both produce a file that breaks the job: the
# first fails --require-hashes on the runner when pip installs a package the
# file does not list, the second pins a two-major-version DOWNGRADE of the
# proxy under test. So the set is resolved with the markers evaluated for the
# target, and checked for self-consistency, by scripts/resolve_windows_pins.py.
#
# FIVE version choices in here are forced and must not be hand-edited or
# bumped on their own. mitmproxy 12.2.3 constrains four of its dependencies,
# three of them to an EXACT version, and a pin above any of those caps makes
# the install unresolvable -- `pip --require-hashes` then fails the whole step,
# not the one package:
#
#     cryptography<=48.1,>=42.0      -> 48.0.1
#     h2<=4.3.0,>=4.3.0              -> 4.3.0    (exact)
#     msgpack<=1.1.2,>=1.0.0         -> 1.1.2    (exact ceiling)
#     tornado<=6.5.5,>=6.5.0         -> 6.5.5    (exact ceiling)
#
# Each of those four is already the NEWEST release the cap admits, so no
# bump is available from inside this file -- they are at the ceiling, not
# behind it. They move when mitmproxy's own cap moves, which means the way to
# advance them is to bump mitmproxy and re-resolve, never to bump them
# directly. mitmproxy 12.2.3 is itself the newest release (checked
# 2026-10-03), so there is no re-resolve waiting to be done either.
#
# WHAT STAYING AT THESE CAPS ACCEPTS. "At the ceiling" is not the same as
# "nothing is accepted", and this block exists because the earlier wording
# here said no security headroom was being given up, which reads as the
# latter. All four caps now sit BELOW a published fix, so holding them
# accepts 15 distinct advisories. Measured 2026-10-03 against OSV and PyPI:
#
#   cryptography==48.0.1  cap <=48.1. No release exists in (48.0.1, 48.1],
#                         so this is the ceiling. 3 advisories, fixes above:
#                         GHSA-jwv3-5hgf-82ww (HIGH, 49.0.0),
#                         GHSA-m2h6-j472-rp4c (MODERATE, 49.0.0),
#                         GHSA-g6cj-pr64-35w5 (HIGH, 50.0.0)
#   h2==4.3.0             cap is exact. 1 advisory:
#                         GHSA-6hr6-w5qg-qmwg (MODERATE, 4.4.1)
#   msgpack==1.1.2        cap is exact. 1 advisory:
#                         GHSA-6v7p-g79w-8964 (HIGH, 1.2.1)
#   tornado==6.5.5        cap is exact, and this is the big one: 10
#                         advisories, every fix in 6.5.6-6.5.9 (latest
#                         6.5.10). HIGH: GHSA-3x9g-8vmp-wqvf (6.5.6),
#                         GHSA-mgf9-4vpg-hj56 (6.5.6), GHSA-mpf4-983q-p7j4
#                         (6.5.8), GHSA-c2m8-h5v5-343r (6.5.9),
#                         GHSA-chx6-46f5-w4vp (6.5.9). MODERATE:
#                         GHSA-pw6j-qg29-8w7f (6.5.7), GHSA-8423-8fgw-73vq
#                         (6.5.8), GHSA-3hv7-mjh2-fv65 (6.5.9). LOW:
#                         GHSA-cx3h-4qpv-8hc9 (6.5.6), GHSA-wwv5-g3v4-889x
#                         (6.5.8)
#
# Eight of the 15 are HIGH, so this is a real acceptance rather than a
# formality. What makes it tolerable is the boundary, not the severities:
# this file is installed by exactly one job (windows-enterprise-tls.yml) on
# one ephemeral Windows runner, and mitmproxy is the TEST HARNESS there -- it
# plays the corporate interception proxy in front of `clawmetry doctor`. It
# runs as `mitmdump --listen-port 8080` bound to loopback, and its only
# client is that same job's `clawmetry doctor` (HTTPS_PROXY=
# http://127.0.0.1:8080). Nothing here ships in a released wheel or reaches a
# user machine, the listener is not reachable off the runner, and the job
# takes `contents: read` with `persist-credentials: false`.
#
# The tornado ten are the clearest case: tornado is mitmproxy's dependency
# for mitmweb, its web UI, and this job starts mitmdump -- the headless tool
# -- so no tornado server is ever listening. The rest describe a server
# handling untrusted clients or a verifier fed untrusted chains, neither of
# which is this job's shape. Treat the list as accepted-and-unreachable
# HERE, not as generally harmless: any new call site for this file has to
# re-argue the boundary, because the pins cannot move while the cap holds.
#
# This acceptance ends when mitmproxy raises a cap. Re-run
# `python3 scripts/resolve_windows_pins.py --write` after any mitmproxy
# bump; that is the one action that clears any of these 15, and the only
# correct one. Do NOT hand-edit a version above its cap to clear an audit
# finding: `pip --require-hashes` fails the whole step, which is how the
# 2026-09-26 group bump broke this job for six days.
#   * cryptography's cap is also why the job tolerates a downgrade mid-install:
#     the job installs clawmetry first, which floors cryptography higher, so
#     pip steps it back down during this install. That is pre-existing
#     behaviour (mitmproxy has always capped it) and this file does not change
#     it.
#   * pyOpenSSL is 26.2.0 rather than newest, because the newest floors
#     cryptography at >=49 and deadlocks against that same <=48.1 cap.
#
# Dependabot does NOT know about these caps: it reads this file, not
# mitmproxy's metadata, and its group bump on 2026-09-26 raised all four past
# them at once. A `dependency-name` ignore cannot express the rule either,
# because it would apply to the whole /.github/requirements directory, where
# eleven other files pin cryptography and legitimately want the newest. The
# guard is instead that this file is in windows-enterprise-tls.yml's
# `paths:` trigger, so a bump to it has to run the job that proves it installs.
#
# Regenerating (targets the job's platform, not the local one):
#   python3 scripts/resolve_windows_pins.py --write
